Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Because there are avenues Of traffic lights, a phone book Of brothers and lawyers, Why should you think your purse Will not be tugged from your arm Or the screen door Will remain latched Against the man Who hugs and kisses His pillow In the corridor of loneliness? There is a window of light A sprinkler turning As the earth turns, And you do not think of the hills And of the splintered wrists it takes To give you The heat rising toward the ceiling. You expect your daughter To be at the door any moment And your husband to arrive With the night That is suddenly all around. You expect the stove to burst A collar of fire When you want it, The siamese cats To move against your legs, purring. But remember this: Because blood revolves from one lung to the next, Why think it will After tonight?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Because, Why, Will

outputs.L1:
Because there are avenues of traffic lights,  
a phone book of brothers and lawyers,  
why should you think your purse  
will not be tugged from your arm,  
or that the screen door  
will remain latched  
against the man  
who hugs and kisses  
his pillow  
in the corridor of loneliness?

There is a window of light,  
a sprinkler turning  
as the earth turns,  
and you do not think of the hills  
or of the splintered wrists it takes  
to give you  
the heat rising toward the ceiling.

You expect your daughter  
to be at the door at any moment,  
and your husband to arrive  
with the night  
that is suddenly all around.

You expect the stove to burst  
into a collar of fire  
when you want it,  
the Siamese cats  
to move against your legs, purring.

But remember this:  
Because blood revolves  
from one lung to the next,  
why think it will  
after tonight?
outputs.L2:
Since boulevards are strung with signals  
and the directory overflows with brothers and attorneys,  
what makes you believe no one will wrench  
the handbag from your shoulder,  
or that the screen door’s latch will keep out  
the man who, alone in the hallway,  
embraces his pillow and covers it with kisses?

A bright window shines.  
A sprinkler circles while the planet spins.  
Yet you give no thought to the hills  
or to the shattered wrists required  
to send warmth climbing toward your ceiling.

You assume your daughter  
will appear at the entrance at any second,  
and that your husband will come home  
along with the darkness  
that has abruptly surrounded everything.

You trust the stove to flare up  
with a ring of flame whenever you ask,  
and the Siamese cats to brush, purring,  
against your legs.

But do not forget:  
though blood keeps circulating  
from one lung to the other,  
why are you certain it will continue  
beyond this night?
outputs.L3:
The poem challenges the assumption that everyday safety and security can be taken for granted. Within the home, familiar routines and domestic comforts create a reassuring sense of stability. People expect their loved ones to return, the household to remain intact, and ordinary necessities such as warmth, food, and shelter to continue being available. Because these expectations are reinforced by habit, they can easily appear permanent.

However, the poem contrasts this protected domestic world with the loneliness, violence, and exhausting labor that exist beyond it. This contrast reveals that comfort is neither universal nor secure: while some people experience the home as a place of refuge, others remain exposed to hardship and danger. Images of darkness and fire further unsettle the apparent safety of ordinary life. They suggest both external threats and the possibility of sudden destruction, emphasizing how quickly familiar circumstances can change.

Ultimately, the poem presents human existence as fundamentally fragile. It moves from questioning social and domestic security to confronting physical vulnerability itself. Even the body’s most basic functions cannot be assumed to continue indefinitely. In this way, the poem warns readers against complacency, reminding them that comfort, safety, and life itself are temporary conditions rather than guarantees.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores how easily the ordinary sense of safety that shapes daily life can be disrupted. Familiar domestic routines and expectations initially suggest comfort, order, and continuity: home appears to be a protected space, and repeated actions create the impression that tomorrow will resemble today. Yet these reassuring images are placed beside references to crime, loneliness, exhausting labor, and bodily vulnerability. Through these contrasts, the poem reveals that security is never absolute. Danger may enter spaces that seem private, companionship may give way to isolation, work may wear down the body, and physical life itself may fail.

This tension between routine and uncertainty gives the poem much of its emotional force. Everyday habits often allow people to live as though stability were guaranteed. Meals are prepared, tasks are completed, and the body continues its familiar rhythms without conscious effort. The poem, however, exposes the assumptions beneath those patterns. Domestic comfort can conceal fear, social order can coexist with violence, and apparent independence can mask emotional or physical need. What seems dependable is therefore shown to be temporary and contingent.

The poem’s images of the body are especially important because they bring its larger concerns into an intimate, unavoidable form. The body is both the means through which daily life is experienced and a reminder that such experience has limits. It can become tired, injured, exposed, or suddenly silent. In this way, bodily vulnerability connects the poem’s images of labor, isolation, and danger to its meditation on death. Mortality is not presented as a distant abstraction but as a possibility already present within ordinary life.

By the conclusion, the poem suggests that even the most reliable rhythms can stop without warning. The routines that seem to promise permanence do not protect anyone from change or death; they merely make continuity feel natural. The final insight is therefore unsettling: safety, comfort, and regularity are real but temporary, and their familiarity can create the illusion that they will last forever. By breaking that illusion, the poem asks readers to recognize both the fragility of everyday existence and the value of the ordinary moments that cannot be guaranteed.
outputs.L5:
**Because, Why, Will**

“Why?” is the question that opens the door to understanding. “Because” offers a reason, even when the answer is incomplete. “Will” looks toward the future and turns ideas into action.

We ask **why** because we are curious. We search for answers **because** knowledge helps us grow. And we use our **will** to continue, even when the path ahead is uncertain. Together, these words represent curiosity, understanding, and determination.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about the fragility of suburban safety, contrasting ordinary domestic comforts with crime, loneliness, hidden labor, and sudden death.
counterfactuals.output:
At dusk, the sprinklers begin  
their silver rehearsal—  
each lawn bowing under a clean rain  
paid for, timed, expected.

Inside, the refrigerator hums  
beside a calendar of soccer games,  
dentist appointments,  
a coupon clipped for detergent.

The deadbolt turns with a small assurance.  
The porch light makes its yellow promise.  
Someone sets the alarm  
and carries warm laundry upstairs.

But beyond the curtains  
a siren opens the night.

Blue light travels over split-level roofs,  
over hydrangeas and minivans,  
over the woman cleaning offices downtown  
who will return at two  
to wake her children at six.

In the house next door  
an old man eats from one plate,  
the television speaking for hours  
without asking him anything.

A teenager scrolls beneath a blanket,  
watching strangers appear loved.  
A mother counts cash at the kitchen table.  
A father circles a bruise  
with the sleeve of his work shirt.

Someone tests car doors  
along the sleeping street.

Someone lies still  
behind a garage with its tools  
hung neatly in outline—  
rake, hammer, shovel—  
everything in its proper place  
except the body.

Morning will come carefully.

Garage doors will rise.  
Coffee will darken the kitchens.  
Packages will wait on porches  
like harmless offerings.

A neighbor will say  
nothing like this happens here,

while workers in bright vests  
lift what has broken,  
wash the pavement,  
trim the hedges back from the signs.

And the sprinklers will begin again,  
turning and turning,  
casting their brief glass over the grass—

each shining drop  
holding the whole street upside down,

then vanishing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, surreal poem addressed to a woman who assumes her home, family, and body will continue functioning normally, ending with a warning about mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
You trust the house because it remembers  
the small religion of morning—  
pipes muttering behind the walls,  
the kettle lifting its silver cry,  
stairs holding their breath beneath your feet.

You trust the photographs to keep their faces.  
Your children orbit the table like bright moons;  
your husband sleeps with one hand open,  
as if nothing could be taken  
without first waking him.

Even your body seems obedient:  
the heart’s red animal pacing its cage,  
the lungs folding and unfolding  
their pale umbrellas,  
your blood carrying its dark baskets  
from room to room.

But under the floorboards, night is growing teeth.  
The mirrors have begun rehearsing emptiness.  
A black orchard roots itself in the cellar,  
bearing clocks instead of fruit,  
each one ripening toward silence.

One evening the lamp will forget your name.  
The hallway will lengthen into winter.  
Those you love will become doors  
you cannot follow through,  
and your faithful flesh will turn strange—  
a house locking you outside.

Do not mistake repetition for mercy,  
nor warmth for permanence.  
Woman, listen: everything that serves you  
is already learning how to stop,  
and death is nearer than the next breath  
you have not yet been promised.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary American poem that begins “Because there are avenues” and uses images of traffic lights, a stolen purse, sprinklers, a stove, Siamese cats, and blood circulating through the lungs.
counterfactuals.output:
Because there are avenues  
we have not crossed, the traffic lights  
keep changing without us—green  
to yellow to the red eye of consequence.  

Someone runs past holding a stolen purse,  
its bright clasp flashing like a small emergency.  
Across the street, sprinklers tick  
over lawns already wet with morning.  

In an upstairs kitchen, a stove clicks on.  
Blue flame gathers beneath a dented pot  
while two Siamese cats watch from the sill,  
their faces dark as unanswered doors.  

The city breathes in buses, bills, sirens,  
breathes out coffee steam and exhaust.  
Inside each stranger, blood circulates  
through the lungs, turning toward oxygen,  

turning again toward the difficult heart—  
as if the body, too, obeyed intersections,  
as if every red light carried the promise  
that something, eventually, will move.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an ominous monologue in poetic form that questions why people trust everyday routines and conveniences when violence and death can interrupt them at any moment.
counterfactuals.output:
Why do you trust the kettle’s little hymn,  
the hallway light, the faithful turning key?  
Why set your shoes beside the door  
as if tomorrow signed its name in ink?

You count on trains to keep their time,  
on bread to rise, on screens to glow,  
on morning waiting patiently  
behind the curtain’s darkened fold.

But violence does not knock.

It enters through the smallest pause—  
a siren threading through a song,  
a shadow where no shadow stood,  
a hand that closes, hard and sudden,  
over the mouth of an ordinary day.

And death—  
death has no reverence for calendars.  
It does not care that coffee cools,  
that laundry turns, that someone promised  
to be home before the rain.

Still, you polish every ritual:  
the lock, the list, the kiss goodbye—  
small charms arranged against the void,  
thin walls of habit, warm and bright.

Tell me:  
when did convenience become a covenant?  
When did routine become a shield?

Listen.

Beneath the clocks, another rhythm waits—  
patient, uninvited, close.  
And every harmless moment balances  
upon a blade too fine to see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a single-stanza free-verse poem in a mid-century confessional style, moving from urban danger to domestic expectation and concluding with the possibility that the speaker may not survive the night.
counterfactuals.output:
The street keeps its knives under the rain,  
each window an eye that has forgotten mercy.  
I walk quickly past the bar’s red mouth,  
past sirens stitching and unstitching the dark,  
carrying my small name like contraband.  
At home they will expect the blue bowl on the table,  
the children’s socks paired, the roast forgiving in its pan,  
my smile pinned neatly above the sink.  
I can already hear the clock rehearsing blame,  
the house breathing through its locked doors.  
But the night has followed me upstairs,  
has laid its cold hand over mine,  
and by morning they may find the bed unslept in,  
the curtains open, the city still burning—  
and no one left in me to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
